Date: 2026-05-14

Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Zhou (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (NovaGuard VP Eng), Priya Rao (SRE Manager), Derek Lin (Cloud Architect)
summary: Discovery call to map NovaGuard's incident tolerance requirements. Discussed multi-region routing, automatic failover, graceful degradation, SLO targets, data residency and security expectations for Private/Dedicated vs Hosted. Agreed next steps: share security pack, deliver failover diagram, confirm traffic profile, set pilot window.
topics: SLA/SLO expectations and P99 vs P95 targets
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs

transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on this account. We also have Lena, our solutions engineer. Could each of you intro quick?
[00:00:12] Carlos Mendez: Yeah Carlos here, VP engineering at NovaGuard. We run security orchestration workloads and increasingly embedding LLM assistants for incident triage.
[00:00:22] Priya Rao: Priya, SRE manager, primarily responsible for uptime for our infra and service degradation playbooks.
[00:00:27] Derek Lin: Derek, cloud architect, mainly looking at networking and region failover configs.
[00:00:33] Lena Zhou: Hi all, Lena. I'll be diving into technical fallbacks and autoscale behavior today.
[00:00:38] Samir Patel: Great. High level, NovaGuard is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — this call focused on resiliency: fallbacks, multi-region routing, SLA expectations, right?
[00:00:47] Carlos Mendez: Exactly. We need to understand how your platform behaves when a region goes noisy or an entire zone degrades. We care about hard SLAs for our security products.
[00:00:58] Lena Zhou: Cool, I'll walk through common incident scenarios we see customers design for and then map to Redwood capabilities.
[00:01:05] Lena Zhou: Scenario A: single-node GPU failure inside a Dedicated pool. We support automatic re-routing to warm capacity or to a compatible model variant. That transition is designed to be quick but there can be a latency bump.
[00:01:20] Derek Lin: Quick meaning — seconds? tens of seconds? We have a 500ms P95 target for user-facing triage responses.
[00:01:28] Lena Zhou: Realistically you'll see per-request increase while KV cache is repopulated, so initial requests could hit a few seconds depending on cold KV warming. But if you enable prefix caching and local KV sticky cache at the edge, steady-state 95th is still low — under 800ms typical for trimmed sequences.
[00:01:45] Priya Rao: When you say local KV sticky cache at the edge — is that something in Hosted? For Private we want to control the cache invalidation window.
[00:01:54] Lena Zhou: We expose cache TTL controls in both Hosted and Private. For Dedicated, your redis/KV sits in the same VPC or can be managed by Redwood depending on the deployment choice. Worth noting sometimes the transcripting engine wrote Redwood Privat in our docs, it's Redwood Private, sorry for the typo.
[00:02:09] Carlos Mendez: No worries.
[00:02:12] Samir Patel: Another common pattern: multi-region routing. We can do active-active across two regions or active-passive. For active-active, requests are routed by geo and load, and we maintain consistent model family versions across regions.
[00:02:25] Derek Lin: How do you handle cross-region KV coherence? If we shard by tenant, we want deterministic fallback to the other region without losing context.
[00:02:34] Lena Zhou: Good question. We don't replicate full KV in real time across region by default — that's expensive. Typical approach is sticky KV by tenant/region + warm start with compacted context sent on failover. So when region B takes over, the client or the router attaches a compacted prefix and recent KV pointers. That increases token cost but preserves safety.
[00:02:51] Priya Rao: That implies a short window of degraded context? For incident triage that can be okay if we mark the response as degraded and show a confidence tag.
[00:03:00] Samir Patel: Exactly. We often recommend a graceful degradation policy: during failover, switch to a cheaper/robust model variant or increase sampling temperature or return structured fallback that indicates partial context. Lena can show what that looks like in logs.
[00:03:14] Lena Zhou: I'll share a snippet in the followup. Another mechanism is automatic fallback tiers — Redwood supports route-level fallback chains. Example: primary model (high-precision), fallback model (quantized lower mem), then a cached static response for extreme outages.
[00:03:29] Carlos Mendez: What's the SLAs around those fallbacks? Our legal asks for uptime guarantees for the endpoint.
[00:03:36] Samir Patel: For Hosted we publish SLA tiers. Dedicated has contractual SLAs with 99.9% uptime for reserved capacity; Private is negotiable but typical enterprise agreements reach 99.95 with specific runbooks. The important bit is how we define availability — API reachable and returning successful responses vs returning degraded-quality responses.
[00:03:55] Derek Lin: We need clarity on what counts as a violation. If API responds within 200ms but with a fallback canned answer, is that an SLA breach?
[00:04:05] Lena Zhou: It's a policy decision. We can surface metrics: percentage of responses that are fallback vs primary. Many customers treat fallback rate above X% as an incident trigger rather than an SLA breach. We'll help you configure SLOs and alerts in the Console.
[00:04:19] Priya Rao: We do want per-tenant fallback histograms and token-level cost breakdowns. Also audit trails for any model variant swap.
[00:04:27] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood Console has token-level cost, per-route histograms, and tracing hooks that record model variant, fallback reason, and origin region. Those logs can be forwarded to your SIEM and we can ship them to a customer S3 bucket or to your Splunk.
[00:04:40] Carlos Mendez: Security stuff — KMS/HSM? We need customer-managed keys for Private deployments.
[00:04:47] Lena Zhou: Private supports KMS integration and HSM-backed key stores. Hosted can integrate with cloud KMS but keys are in the customer's managed account in most cases. We'll provide a security pack with our encryption at rest/in transit detail.
[00:04:58] Derek Lin: And identity — SSO/SAML, RBAC? Auditing on who rolled a model?
[00:05:03] Samir Patel: SSO via SAML/OIDC and role-based controls are available. The audit log includes change events: model rollouts, canary promotions, fallback policy edits. We also export the audit stream to customer-managed logging.
[00:05:14] Priya Rao: Latency budgets — we have a user facing 500ms P95, user tolerance up to 2s for P99 maybe. How would Redwood help guarantee that under heavy load?
[00:05:26] Lena Zhou: We recommend Dedicated with reserved GPU pools sized to your peak qps plus burst. Autoscaling and burst capacity are configurable. For low-latency critical paths, we suggest using dedicated warm nodes with larger batch windows tuned to keep tail low. There's a tradeoff: bigger batching reduces token cost but can add latency jitter.
[00:05:43] Derek Lin: So batching vs latency tradeoff — can we set per-route max-latency or prefer latency SLO over cost?
[00:05:50] Lena Zhou: Yes, route-level policies allow you to set routing by latency SLO (route to low-latency pool), or cost SLO (route to quantized cheaper model). There's also automatic fallback if latency spikes past thresholds.
[00:05:59] Carlos Mendez: About model versions — if we pin a model in Dedicated, can you do canary traffic to new model in Hosted and then promote? We want safe rollouts.
[00:06:08] Samir Patel: Absolutely. Rollouts support canary, A/B and automatic rollback policies based on latency or quality regression. We integrate with your eval sets to guard against quality dips.
[00:06:18] Priya Rao: In an incident when you roll back, are previous model artifacts still accessible for audit? We need to answer auditors.
[00:06:24] Lena Zhou: Yes, model versioning and artifact manifests are stored with immutable IDs. Audit logs show which version served each request and when it was rolled back.
[00:06:32] Derek Lin: Network failover specifics — does Redwood manage BGP announcements or do we rely on DNS TTLs? We can't accept 30-second DNS waits.
[00:06:41] Lena Zhou: We use smart routing with health checks and can route at the edge using Anycast plus routing policy; in Private deployments you can front Redwood with your own load balancer and we support active health probes and control plane signals for faster switchovers. For Hosted we maintain regional endpoints and recommend low TTLs for critical services plus warm cross-region capacity.
[00:06:59] Carlos Mendez: If a whole cloud region has a provider outage, what's the recommended path?
[00:07:05] Samir Patel: Multi-region active-passive with warm standby is simplest: replicate state periodically, have compacted prefixes for prompt warm starts, and have routing that flips to standby region automatically. For stricter RTOs we support active-active with session affinity and best-effort KV replication patterns.
[00:07:21] Priya Rao: What's the expected RTO for active-passive?
[00:07:24] Lena Zhou: Depends on how you trade cost: with warm standby and pre-warmed KV, failover can be sub-90 seconds for most workloads; with cold starts it can be minutes.
[00:07:33] Derek Lin: Okay that's useful.
[00:07:36] Carlos Mendez: Let's talk about billing implications during failover. If we route to a more expensive hot region, do you credit us for the cost delta if it was a platform outage?
[00:07:45] Samir Patel: Billing adjustments are negotiable in enterprise contracts. For Hosted standard terms we advertise pricing and overage; for Dedicated/Private we can include burn-rate offsets or incident credits in the SLA. We'll document options in the pricing sheet.
[00:07:58] Priya Rao: We are also concerned about data residency during failover. Some tenant data can't leave EU. How do you prevent cross-border failover?
[00:08:06] Lena Zhou: Route policies can be scoped by tenant and geography. If a tenant is EU-only, you can mark it as no-cross-region-failover; in an extreme outage you could opt for degraded service within region rather than cross-border failover.
[00:08:18] Derek Lin: That would be our preference for regulated customers.
[00:08:21] Samir Patel: Good note. We'll include that in the failover diagram.
[00:08:24] Lena Zhou: Now a bit on observability: we log fallback reason codes, model variant, region, and fallback chain. You get dashboards and alerts for increase in fallback rate, latency tail, and KV miss rate.
[00:08:36] Carlos Mendez: Do you have an example alert threshold you'd recommend?
[00:08:39] Lena Zhou: Typical: fallback rate > 3% for 5 minutes triggers P0; P99 latency > 2s for 3 minutes triggers P0. We'll tune to your traffic profile.
[00:08:48] Priya Rao: For the pilot, we want to run a simulated region outage and observe behavior end-to-end. Can Redwood help orchestrate that test?
[00:08:56] Samir Patel: Yes, we do incident injection assist in pilots. We can coordinate a failover window and capture traces. That's a great way to validate SLOs.
[00:09:04] Carlos Mendez: Great. A few questions from legal/security: do you provide SOC 2 Type II, Pen testing reports, data processing appendix for EU?
[00:09:12] Samir Patel: We'll share our full security pack — SOC2 Type II, penetration test summaries, DPA template, and private deployment compliance options.
[00:09:20] Derek Lin: One more detail — can you throttle or queue requests per-tenant during pressure so that a noisy tenant doesn't stomp on neighbors?
[00:09:27] Lena Zhou: Yes, per-tenant rate limiting and soft QoS tiers are supported. We also provide backpressure signals and circuit breakers at the route level.
[00:09:35] Carlos Mendez: Any known gotchas we should watch for when migrating from an existing self-hosted transformer stack?
[00:09:41] Lena Zhou: Watch tokenization and prompt casing differences across model variants; also KV warm-up patterns and cold-start latencies. We'll supply migration guidance and reference terraform for Dedicated and Private.
[00:09:53] Priya Rao: Okay, let's recap next steps.
[00:09:56] Samir Patel: Recap: I'll send security pack and SOC2 artifacts. Lena will produce a multi-region failover diagram with suggested routing and fallback tiers. NovaGuard will share traffic profile and tenant restrictions. We'll propose a pilot week w/ incident injection. Any other asks?
[00:10:11] Carlos Mendez: Please include sample audit log format.
[00:10:14] Derek Lin: And include expected token cost during failovers for budgeting.
[00:10:18] Samir Patel: Noted. We'll include cost delta estimates.
[00:10:22] Priya Rao: Thanks, this was useful.
[00:10:24] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials this week and schedule the pilot window after we get traffic numbers.
[00:10:32] [END]
